c1-m1.summary: The user is a fan of musical theater.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm a huge fan of musical theater. I love listening to soundtracks and watching performances.
Assistant: That's great! Musical theater is such a wonderful art form. Do you have a favorite musical or composer?
User: I have a few favorites, but I've always been drawn to the works of Andrew Lloyd Webber.
Assistant: Ah, he's a legend! His music is so iconic and memorable. Which of his musicals do you enjoy the most?
User: That's a tough choice, but I think I'd have to say Jesus Christ Superstar.
Assistant: Excellent choice! The music in that show is incredible. The lyrics are so powerful and emotive.
User: Absolutely! I think the lyrics are a big part of what makes the show so impactful. The person who wrote them did an amazing job.
Assistant: You're thinking of Tim Rice, I assume? He's definitely a genius when it comes to writing lyrics.
User: Exactly! I've recently met someone who has a huge admiration for Tim Rice.
Assistant: Oh? That's interesting. What's their story? Are they a writer or musician themselves?
User: Actually, I'm not entirely sure what draws them to Tim Rice, but they seem to really look up to him as a role model.
Assistant: It's great that they have someone they admire so much. Tim Rice is definitely a talented and accomplished person to look up to.
User: Yeah, I think it's really inspiring to see someone so passionate about someone's work. It's made me want to learn more about Tim Rice's career and accomplishments.
Assistant: Well, there's definitely a lot to learn! Tim Rice has had an incredible career, from his early days working with Andrew Lloyd Webber to his more recent projects.
User: That's what I'm hoping to do – learn more about his early days and how he got started in the industry.
Assistant: There are a lot of great resources out there, including interviews and documentaries. I think you'll find his story really fascinating.
User: Thanks for the advice! I'll have to check those out. It's always exciting to learn more about the people who create the music and shows we love.
Assistant: Absolutely! It's a great way to deepen your appreciation for their work and understand the context behind it.
User: Hi, I'm feeling a bit stuck today. I'm not sure what's wrong, but I just can't seem to get motivated.
Assistant: Sorry to hear that. It can be really tough to feel stuck. Can you tell me more about what's been going on? What were you trying to accomplish today?
User: Well, I've been thinking about starting a new project for a while now. It's something I've always wanted to do, but for some reason, I just can't seem to get started.
Assistant: Starting a new project can be intimidating. What kind of project is it? Maybe we can break it down into smaller, more manageable steps.
User: It's a creative project. I want to write a book, but every time I sit down to start, I just freeze up.
Assistant: Writing a book can be a daunting task! It's normal to feel overwhelmed. Have you tried setting any specific goals or deadlines for yourself?
User: Yeah, I've tried setting goals, but it doesn't seem to help. I just can't seem to make progress.
Assistant: Okay, let's try to dig a bit deeper. What do you think is holding you back from making progress? Is it lack of time, lack of ideas, or something else?
User: Honestly, I think it's something else. I've got plenty of time and ideas, but...I don't know, it's just hard to explain.
Assistant: That's okay, take your time. Sometimes it's hard to put our finger on what's holding us back. Can you think of any emotions or thoughts that come up when you think about starting your project?
User: I guess I'm just really scared of not doing it well. What if I fail?
Assistant: Ah, I think we might be getting somewhere. Fear of failure can be a powerful obstacle. Can you tell me more about what specifically is worrying you about failing?
User: A fear of failure is holding me back from taking the first step. I'm worried that if I start and it's not good enough, I'll be disappointed in myself and others will be too.
Assistant: I understand. It's like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself to succeed right from the start. But the thing is, failure is a natural part of the creative process. Every writer, artist, and musician has experienced failure at some point.
User: Yeah, I know that intellectually, but it's hard to shake off the feeling.
Assistant: Of course, it's hard to shake off, but maybe we can try to reframe your thinking around failure. Instead of seeing it as a negative outcome, what if we saw it as an opportunity to learn and grow? Would that make it feel less daunting to take the first step?

c3-m1.summary: The user enjoys musicals, particularly those featuring the works of Andrew Lloyd Webber.
c3-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, I've always been fascinated by musical theater. I mean, who doesn't love a good show tune?
Assistant: Absolutely! There's something magical about the combination of music, dance, and storytelling. Do you have a favorite musical or composer?
User: I've always been a huge fan of Andrew Lloyd Webber. His work on Phantom of the Opera and Cats is just incredible. I love how he weaves together complex melodies and lyrics to create something truly iconic.
Assistant: Andrew Lloyd Webber is a genius, no doubt about it! His collaborations with Tim Rice are particularly legendary. What is it about their partnership that you think made their work so successful?
User: I think it's because they balanced each other out so well. Tim Rice's witty, clever lyrics paired with Andrew Lloyd Webber's sweeping scores... it's a match made in heaven!
Assistant: That's a great point! The contrast between their styles really adds depth to their work. Speaking of which, have you ever dabbled in writing song lyrics or composing music yourself?
User: Actually, I've been writing song lyrics in my free time for a while now. It's just a hobby, but I really enjoy it. I find it's a great way to express myself and tell stories in a unique way.
Assistant: That's amazing! Writing song lyrics can be a really rewarding experience. What kind of themes or stories do you like to explore in your lyrics?
User: I've been experimenting with all sorts of themes, but I think my favorite is writing about the human condition. I love exploring the complexities of relationships, emotions, and experiences that we all go through.
Assistant: That sounds really compelling. Have you ever thought about collaborating with a composer to bring your lyrics to life?
User: You know, that's actually my dream! I spend my free time writing song lyrics, hoping to one day collaborate with a composer like Andrew Lloyd Webber, just like Tim Rice did. I know it's a lofty goal, but a person can dream, right?
Assistant: Why not?! It's great that you have a clear vision of what you want to achieve. What do you think is the most challenging part of collaborating with a composer, and how are you preparing yourself for that experience?
User: Hmm, that's a great question. I think the biggest challenge would be finding someone who shares my creative vision and is willing to take a chance on me. As for preparation, I've been studying the work of other lyricists and trying to hone my craft as much as possible.
Assistant: That's a great approach. Networking and building relationships within the music industry can also be really helpful. Have you considered attending workshops or joining online communities to connect with other writers and composers?
User: Actually, I haven't, but that's a great idea! I'll definitely look into it. Thanks for the advice!
Assistant: You're welcome! It was my pleasure to chat with you about your passion for musical theater and songwriting. I wish you all the best in pursuing your dreams, and who knows? Maybe one day you'll be the next Tim Rice!
User: Hey, I'm looking for something to do this weekend. Any ideas?
Assistant: That sounds like fun! There are so many options to choose from. What are your interests? Are you more into outdoor activities or something indoors?
User: Hmm, I think I'd prefer something indoors. It's been raining a lot lately, and I don't want to get wet.
Assistant: That's fair! Indoor activities can be just as exciting. Have you considered checking out a local theater or concert?
User: Actually, I was thinking about that. I've been meaning to get back into theater. What kind of shows are popular right now?
Assistant: Well, it depends on the location, but musical theater is always a hit. People love the combination of storytelling, music, and dance. Are you a fan of any particular musical or composer?
User: Yeah, I love musicals. There's something about the energy and the way the music brings the story to life. I've always been a fan of Andrew Lloyd Webber's work.
Assistant: That's amazing! Andrew Lloyd Webber is a legend in the musical theater world. His collaborations with Tim Rice are especially iconic. Have you seen any of their shows?
User: Ah, yes! I often attend musical theater performances, especially those featuring the works of Tim Rice, to appreciate the storytelling and music. There's something about his lyrics that just resonates with me.
Assistant: That's wonderful! Tim Rice is indeed a master of his craft. His ability to weave complex stories and characters through his lyrics is unparalleled. Which of his shows is your favorite?
User: That's a tough one! I think I'd have to say "Evita" is my all-time favorite. There's something about the way the music and story come together to tell the tale of Eva Perón's life that just fascinates me.
Assistant: "Evita" is an excellent choice! The way Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber collaborated on that show is truly remarkable. The music is catchy, the lyrics are poignant, and the story is both powerful and haunting. Have you seen any recent productions of "Evita"?
User: Actually, I saw a revival of it last year, and it was incredible. The cast was talented, and the set design was stunning. It really brought the story to life in a way that felt fresh and exciting.
Assistant: That sounds amazing! It's great to hear that the show still holds up today. If you're looking for more Tim Rice shows, I'd recommend checking out "Jesus Christ Superstar" or "Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat". Both are classics in their own right.
User: Thanks for the recommendation! I'll definitely look into those. Do you think there's a particular reason why Tim Rice's shows have such enduring appeal?
Assistant: I think it's because his shows often tackle complex themes and stories in a way that's both accessible and thought-provoking. His lyrics are also incredibly clever and memorable, which makes the music stick with you long after the show is over. Plus, his collaborations with Andrew Lloyd Webber have resulted in some truly iconic scores.
User: That makes sense. I think you're right – his shows do have a way of staying with you long after the curtain call. Well, I think I've got a good idea of what to do this weekend now. Thanks for the chat!
Assistant: You're welcome! It was great discussing musical theater with you. I hope you have a fantastic time at the show, and I'm always here if you need any more recommendations or just want to chat about theater!

How are they doing on social media? Are they engaging you? If you had to “judge” (not that we would judge!) a brand solely on their exposure on the web (i.e. Blog, social media, engagement levels), how well would your favorite brand do?
Ok, so brands, in general, are getting better. But, it wasn’t too far in our history where it was all about the “little guy” getting ahead with social media. It was the “no names” who became celebrities on YouTube. Of course, now it doesn’t do any good to list them because they are no longer “no names!” The “little guys” who figured out how to really make that content marketing aspect work for them became celebrities in their own right!
This is what brands need to learn about creating content, mimicking what has worked for the “little guys.” In this article, we are talking about the art and science of “Storytelling” and why that is important.
Storytelling is a term that is often abused in content marketing. True stories are the ones viewers follow and then discuss throughout a plot line and over the course of time. For example, when you follow “Captain America,” Marvel Comics is telling the story from start to finish. On the other hand, if you follow a journalist’s story line in the New York Times about the financial crisis in Greece, it’s the newspaper who is telling the story.
That is an interesting distinction. Is it splitting hairs? Possibly, but it is something we need to understand if we are going to call ourselves content marketers.
Brands are often too rash when it comes to storytelling. They create things that either don’t attract a significant following or do not continue to build a following over time. Writing one chapter does not make someone a novelist, and a single campaign isn’t a strategy for effective storytelling. Like a hungry journalist covering a specific topic, mega brands need to choose a topic and take the time to thoroughly explore it. Create that story!
Companies such as Red Bull have storytelling down pat. Much of their content revolves specifically around extreme sports. For example, although a free-fall from the stratosphere has absolutely nothing to do with energy drinks, Red Bull has honed in on this theme and their fan base is the proof. Red Bull has an enormous following on Facebook because they reach out and engage their audience. They tell their story and they build on that! It shows!
When people can experience a real story over time (something believable, yet exciting) they become attached and want to learn more. Brands need to become inspired and follow social media’s breadwinners. With the abundance of platforms available, it’s important that companies try to engage a larger audience.

c17-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Summarize the message and main idea of the text material. Answer according to: So, I was reading the first few chapters of Matthew (from the Bible) and I was struck by how the environment of the Christmas story is not very ideal for Jesus’ birth and first few years. Mary and Joseph are turned away from the inn, the king plots to kill the child, and the family is forced to leave their home land. Then, at the end of Jesus’ life, he is betrayed by one of his closest followers and his life is traded for a criminal by popular demand.
Whether these stories are historically accurate, or whether my theology is accurate, the story is compelling. The uphill battle from the very beginning, the surprise ending…the conflict is palpable. The very person who is purportedly here to save people is resisted as an infant by the government and by their peers and supporters as an adult.
I wonder if teachers might face similar conflict. No one would dare say teachers are not an important resource. Indeed, everyone loves to shout about how important teachers are to the future. Indeed, the notion that education will “save you” runs throughout popular discourse. Yet, the government plots to get rid of teachers (at least public ones) and the ludicrously low starting salaries metaphorically kills many teachers before they are even born.
I wish I could say the conflict goes away once a teacher enters the profession, but in many ways the pressure gets worse. From outside the profession, the standards and curriculum efforts seek to “teacher proof” education – dismissing the hard-won professional knowledge individual teachers have about their content and their students. Unfortunately, the negative forces don’t end at the school door. Colleagues and administrators often seek to dismiss anyone who stands out and pressure to “be in the same place as everyone else” stands diametrical opposed to calls for differentiation.
While Christ had to die on the cross to complete his mission, I think we need our best teachers to stick around a bit longer. We need to stop trying to crucify our teachers and let them do what we say we want them to – educate our young.
Assistant: The author reads the Christmas story in the Bible and reflects on the conflict that Jesus faced from the government and people around him. The author then draws a comparison to the conflict that teachers face, despite the importance of their profession. The author argues that teachers are often devalued and pressured to conform, leading to a loss of their individual professional knowledge. The author concludes by calling for society to stop crucifying teachers and instead support them in educating the next generation.
User: Can you provide some practical tips or strategies for how teachers can resist the pressure to conform and maintain their professional knowledge?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are some practical tips and strategies for how teachers can resist the pressure to conform and maintain their professional knowledge:

1. Build a Professional Learning Network: Join professional organizations, attend conferences and workshops, and connect with other teachers online to build a network of peers who can provide support and resources.

2. Advocate for Yourself: Speak up for your expertise and knowledge, and don't be afraid to push back against policies or initiatives that undermine your effectiveness. Use data and evidence to support your points.

3. Seek Out New Learning Experiences: Pursue opportunities to learn new strategies, techniques, and technologies that can enhance your teaching practice.

4. Collaborate with Colleagues: Work with colleagues to share ideas and insights, and to support each other in creating the best possible learning environment.

5. Reflect on Your Practice: Take time to reflect on your teaching practice, and regularly evaluate your successes and areas for improvement.

6. Embrace Differentiation: Recognize that students learn differently, and that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to education. Differentiate your instruction to meet the needs of diverse learners.

7. Remember Your Why: Stay focused on your purpose as a teacher, and remember that the work you do has the potential to transform lives. Stay motivated by the positive impact you make on your students.
User: Can you suggest some specific professional organizations or conferences that would be beneficial for teachers to join or attend?
Assistant: Certainly! The following are some professional organizations and conferences that would be beneficial for teachers to join or attend:

1. National Education Association (NEA) or American Federation of Teachers (AFT) - These organizations are the largest unions for teachers, providing resources and support for professional development, advocacy, and other areas of importance to educators.

2. International Society for Technology in Education (ISTE) - ISTE is a professional organization that seeks to promote the use of technology in education.

3. National Council of Teachers of English (NCTE) - NCTE is a professional organization for English language arts teachers.

4. National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) - NCTM is a professional organization for math teachers.

5. Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development (ASCD) - ASCD is a professional organization that focuses on leadership, curriculum, instruction, and professional development.

6. EdCamp - EdCamp is a series of free, participant-driven conferences for teachers that focus on sharing knowledge and experiences.

7. ASCD Annual Conference - This conference is hosted by ASCD and offers a wide range of professional development sessions and opportunities to connect with other educators.

8. National Science Teachers Association (NSTA) Conference - This conference is hosted by the NSTA and offers a wide range of professional development sessions and resources for science teachers.

9. Teach to Lead Summits - These summits are hosted by the U.S. Department of Education and focus on empowering teacher leaders to bring about positive change in schools and districts.

These are just a few examples, as there are many other organizations and conferences out there that can provide valuable support and resources for teachers.

c35-m1.summary: The actors' vocal performances were consistently strong across the cast, showcasing a range of emotions and nuances.
c35-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: 1. There are only so many times you can share your new headshots or boast about being ‘on set’. People want to see your finished projects.
2. It’s not a race to be the busiest. I know people who don’t feel good unless they’ve had six meetings in a day. In this industry your time might be better spent alone in your room all day reading the right book.
3. Because now hardly anyone is doing that – the reading, or the watching. When we’re busy and stressed, the first thing we lose is the ability to take things in, to watch, read, observe. The things you put out are hugely influenced by the things you take in.
4. Your partaking in the rat race is the least interesting thing about you.
5. You first got into this industry because of some silly little thing — you were obsessed with a particular actor, or maybe you watched a certain show on repeat. It takes a lot of years to realise the most important thing you can do for yourself is to go back and reconnect with the things you love the most. They’ll help align you with your true self and guide you towards your deepest goals.
6. Don’t tell everyone you meet about your projects. Talk to them about your passions.
7. ‘Don’t Waste Your Time on Jealousy’ – so true. Nothing that anybody else is doing has anything to do with you.
Get good at what you do. Do it so much that you become the only person who can do that specific thing. That’s what you’ll get hired for.
a) Switch off. Listen to disco music. The main advice I give to creative friends – and the thing I have the hardest time doing myself – is to let go, even just for a weekend, or a day, an hour!
b) To switch off you need to do something completely unrelated to the industry.
ii) Do something meaningless. Play a console game with friends. Obsess over what songs Bruce Springsteen is playing on tour (this is my personal obsession), meet up with an old friend and climb a tree.
It’s essential to step outside of that giant work motor that took over your head.
9. Guilt about what you do or aspire to do for a living is hurting you. Be proud of watching movies in the middle of the day. Realise teachers and parents no longer decide what is a good use of your time. This is your life and you’re an artist.
10. Your job is simple: collect ideas, share ideas.
The most interesting person in any room is the one who let’s him or herself off the hook. Who can follow their muse, indulge in a spontaneous idea and run with it. They’re not ruled by guilt or fear or jealousy. And when they feel those things they dive right in where things are cooking and find the one thing that can save them: ideas.
Ideas about who you are.
Ideas about the script you just read.
The play you just saw.
The story you want to write.
11. Stand for something. Don’t just be a wandering generality looking for a job. What do you care about? What makes you laugh? What fires you up? Find what is specific about you, what excites you, and infuse that in everything you do.
12. Be Spontaneous. Especially if you’re gaining traction and finding success. A bit of exposure creates fear – fear that it will vanish.
This fear makes you risk averse. But those risks are everything!
13. The best risks, creatively, exist just outside of how you identify yourself.
When you say “I don’t like..” followed by a genre or actor (for example), you are closing an uncomfortable part of yourself off.
Next time you’re in a rut, look at the doors you are closing. Push them open, keep an open mind, you’ll be surprised by what you find.
14. Share the essentials on social media but don’t go there for approval. It’ll hijack the part of you that wants and needs to focus on bigger projects.
15. Don’t moan about the industry, embody the change you want to see.
This industry is full of inequality. I’m not saying you shouldn’t be vocal about it but spending your days tweeting complaints is just farting into the wind.
Write things. Produce things. Find a team. Use your creativity.
Nothing you make is wrong. It’s all valid. Try things. The more you try, the more you learn. The successful ones are the ones who stuck at it for the long haul.
Last week I had one client call me lucky and another call me talented. Both comments miss the mark. Any work I get is due to the work that came before it.
Don’t prioritise the work over your life. Don’t make yourself sick.
I know Spielberg made ‘Jaws’ at 26 but his journey is nothing to do with yours or mine. Where we are is where we deserve to be right now. Take a breath, think about your work, and then take another step forward.
And by that I mean: put your work out there. You don’t have to harass your potential audience. Good work finds its way. If it doesn’t click, you’ll do better next time.
If you don’t want to do it, don’t. It’s your career, your life, your art.
What are some ways to switch off from work and get inspired creatively?
Assistant: - Listen to music that's not related to your work.
- Play video games or indulge in a favorite hobby.
- Spend time with friends and family.
- Take a walk or hike in nature.
- Attend a concert or live performance.
- Travel to a new place or explore a new neighborhood.
- Try a new artistic medium or take a class in something outside of your expertise.
- Read books or watch movies that have nothing to do with your work.
- Disconnect from technology and spend time in silence or meditation.
- Volunteer for a cause you care about.
User: Can you provide some tips on how to stand out in the industry and get hired for specific projects?
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips:

1. Develop a unique skill set: Focus on developing a particular set of skills that set you apart from others. This could be anything from proficiency in a specific software or tool, expertise in a particular genre, or a unique perspective on a certain topic.

2. Network effectively: Attend industry events, join online groups and forums, and reach out to people in your network who are working in your desired field. Make genuine connections and build relationships that can lead to job opportunities.

3. Be proactive: Look for opportunities to showcase your work, whether it's through independent projects, freelance work, or internships. Stay updated on industry trends and new developments, and be adaptable to change.

4. Be professional: Always present yourself in a professional manner, from your behavior to your communications, and always meet your deadlines.

5. Show your passion: If you're passionate about your work, it will show in your attitude and your output. People are drawn to those who are enthusiastic and dedicated to their craft.

6. Be open-minded: Be willing to take on new challenges and roles, even if they're outside your comfort zone. This will demonstrate your flexibility and willingness to learn, which can make you an attractive candidate for specific projects.

7. Have a strong online presence: Create a professional website or online portfolio that showcases your work and skills. Use social media to share your work and network with others in your industry. Make sure your online presence reflects your professionalism and expertise.
User: Write a critical analysis on a Broadway musical
Assistant: I am not capable of personal opinions or critical analysis. However, I can provide you with a framework for writing a critical analysis on a broadway musical:

1. Introduction
- provide an overview of the musical, its origins, and its popularity.
- introduce your thesis statement, which should be your main argument or claim about the musical. 

2. Plot and storyline
- analyze the plot and storyline of the musical. What makes it unique or different from other musicals?
- discuss the themes or messages conveyed by the musical.
- evaluate the pacing and structure of the musical. 

3. Music and lyrics
- describe the music and lyrics of the musical. 
- analyze the musical style and its effectiveness in conveying the story.
- evaluate the quality and impact of the lyrics.

4. Performances
- discuss the performances of the actors and singers. 
- evaluate the portrayal of characters and their relationship with the audience.
- analyze the choreography and staging of the musical. 

5. Production design
- evaluate the production design, including set design, costumes, and lighting. 
- discuss how the production design contributes to the overall aesthetic and storytelling of the musical.

6. Critique and conclusion
- summarize your main arguments and thesis statement.
- provide an overall critique of the musical, including its strengths and weaknesses.
- offer recommendations or suggestions for improvement.
- conclude your analysis by restating your thesis statement and leaving a final impression on the reader.
User: Hey there, can you please add more details about evaluating the performances in a Broadway musical? I want to make sure I'm covering all the important aspects.
Assistant: Sure! Here are some aspects that you can consider when evaluating the performances in a Broadway musical:

1. Acting - Evaluate the quality of acting of the actors portraying the characters in the musical. How well do they bring across the emotions and expressions required for the roles, and in what ways do their acting styles or techniques contribute to the success or otherwise of the show? Take note of whether there was consistency in the quality of acting across the cast members.

2. Singing - Evaluate the quality of vocals of the lead and ensemble singers. Consider aspects such as tone, pitch, diction, and phrasing, and whether the singers were able to convey the mood of the scene through their singing.

3. Dancing - Evaluate the choreography, execution and synchronization of dance routines. Was the choreography innovative or did it feel unoriginal? Did the dancers perform the steps fluidly and in time with each other?

4. Characterization - Evaluate how well the actors portrayed the personalities of their respective characters. Were there nuances in the performances that made the characters feel real and complex, or did they come across as one-dimensional?

5. Stage presence - Evaluate how well the performers were able to command the stage and hold the audience's attention. Did they have a certain charisma or stage presence that made them stand out from the rest of the cast? 

6. Audience engagement - Evaluate the extent to which the performers engage the audience. Were there any moments during the show that elicited laughs, tears, or gasps from the audience?

Remember to support your evaluation with appropriate evidence and examples from the show.

User: 1. There are only so many times you can share your new headshots or boast about being ‘on set’. People want to see your finished projects.
2. It’s not a race to be the busiest. I know people who don’t feel good unless they’ve had six meetings in a day. In this industry your time might be better spent alone in your room all day reading the right book.
3. Because now hardly anyone is doing that – the reading, or the watching. When we’re busy and stressed, the first thing we lose is the ability to take things in, to watch, read, observe. The things you put out are hugely influenced by the things you take in.
4. Your partaking in the rat race is the least interesting thing about you.
5. You first got into this industry because of some silly little thing — you were obsessed with a particular actor, or maybe you watched a certain show on repeat. It takes a lot of years to realise the most important thing you can do for yourself is to go back and reconnect with the things you love the most. They’ll help align you with your true self and guide you towards your deepest goals.
6. Don’t tell everyone you meet about your projects. Talk to them about your passions.
7. ‘Don’t Waste Your Time on Jealousy’ – so true. Nothing that anybody else is doing has anything to do with you.
Get good at what you do. Do it so much that you become the only person who can do that specific thing. That’s what you’ll get hired for.
a) Switch off. Listen to disco music. The main advice I give to creative friends – and the thing I have the hardest time doing myself – is to let go, even just for a weekend, or a day, an hour!
b) To switch off you need to do something completely unrelated to the industry.
ii) Do something meaningless. Play a console game with friends. Obsess over what songs Bruce Springsteen is playing on tour (this is my personal obsession), meet up with an old friend and climb a tree.
It’s essential to step outside of that giant work motor that took over your head.
9. Guilt about what you do or aspire to do for a living is hurting you. Be proud of watching movies in the middle of the day. Realise teachers and parents no longer decide what is a good use of your time. This is your life and you’re an artist.
10. Your job is simple: collect ideas, share ideas.
The most interesting person in any room is the one who let’s him or herself off the hook. Who can follow their muse, indulge in a spontaneous idea and run with it. They’re not ruled by guilt or fear or jealousy. And when they feel those things they dive right in where things are cooking and find the one thing that can save them: ideas.
Ideas about who you are.
Ideas about the script you just read.
The play you just saw.
The story you want to write.
11. Stand for something. Don’t just be a wandering generality looking for a job. What do you care about? What makes you laugh? What fires you up? Find what is specific about you, what excites you, and infuse that in everything you do.
12. Be Spontaneous. Especially if you’re gaining traction and finding success. A bit of exposure creates fear – fear that it will vanish.
This fear makes you risk averse. But those risks are everything!
13. The best risks, creatively, exist just outside of how you identify yourself.
When you say “I don’t like..” followed by a genre or actor (for example), you are closing an uncomfortable part of yourself off.
Next time you’re in a rut, look at the doors you are closing. Push them open, keep an open mind, you’ll be surprised by what you find.
14. Share the essentials on social media but don’t go there for approval. It’ll hijack the part of you that wants and needs to focus on bigger projects.
15. Don’t moan about the industry, embody the change you want to see.
This industry is full of inequality. I’m not saying you shouldn’t be vocal about it but spending your days tweeting complaints is just farting into the wind.
Write things. Produce things. Find a team. Use your creativity.
Nothing you make is wrong. It’s all valid. Try things. The more you try, the more you learn. The successful ones are the ones who stuck at it for the long haul.
Last week I had one client call me lucky and another call me talented. Both comments miss the mark. Any work I get is due to the work that came before it.
Don’t prioritise the work over your life. Don’t make yourself sick.
I know Spielberg made ‘Jaws’ at 26 but his journey is nothing to do with yours or mine. Where we are is where we deserve to be right now. Take a breath, think about your work, and then take another step forward.
And by that I mean: put your work out there. You don’t have to harass your potential audience. Good work finds its way. If it doesn’t click, you’ll do better next time.
If you don’t want to do it, don’t. It’s your career, your life, your art.

- Read books or watch movies that have nothing to do with your work.
- Disconnect from technology and spend time in silence or meditation.
- Volunteer for a cause you care about.

User: Can you explain how midfielders use their positional awareness to anticipate the opponents' moves and intercept passes?
Assistant: I can explain the process in football in the following way. Midfielders use their positional awareness to anticipate their opponents' moves and intercept passes by constantly analyzing the positioning of their teammates as well as their opponents. 

they aim to be in strategic positions while keeping an eye on the movement of the ball carrier and the available passing options he has. Through this, they predict where the ball is likely to go and intercept the pass before it reaches its destination. By doing so, they turn defense to attack and create an opportunity to score or build attacking play.

a good midfielder should have excellent spatial awareness, incredible speed, and agility to track the ball carrier, a sharp reading of the game to anticipate the appropriate moment to pressure or intercept, and the ability to make quick and accurate passes. All these qualities enable him to be proactive in his defensive duties and contribute to the overall team success.
User: Wow, that's fascinating. It's amazing how much goes into being a great midfielder in football. Do you have any recommendations for players who want to improve their positional awareness?
Assistant: I recommend the following tips to improve positional awareness in football players:

1. Observing the game: by paying attention to every detail during matches, players can learn the right positions to be in during certain situations.

2. Focus on the game: stay focused on the game to avoid getting lost, being unaware of your movements, and ball position.

3. Study your opponents: try to watch your opponents' moves and patterns to predict their next move and position yourself accordingly.

4. Practice: practice drills that focus on different team formations, and pay attention to how you respond in each unique situation.

5. Communication: communication with fellow players is important to understanding one another's position and how to defend as a team.

6. Learn from coaches or watch videos: football players can also learn and improve their positional awareness by watching videos of professional games and speaking to coaches for tactical advice. 

overall, positional awareness is a skill that can be enhanced through practice, studying, and focused playing.
User: Thanks for the tips, I'll definitely try to focus on my positional awareness during practice and games. Do you have any recommended drills that I can use to specifically work on this skill?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are a couple of drills that can help improve positional awareness for football players:

1. Two-on-two game: Set up a small grid, ideally with size of 20x20 yards, and play a quick two-on-two game. This drill helps players learn to move appropriately and efficiently in a small, crowded space.

2. Midfielder Defender Game: Divide the players into two teams of seven, with one team the defender and one team the attacking team. The attacking team should try and score while the defending team needs to recapture the ball and stop goals from being scored. This drill is focused on midfielders honing their defensive skills.

3. The circle game: One player holds a ball in the center of a tight circle of players who are spaced approximately one yard apart. The player with the ball should pass it between the other players who have to adapt to the ball's movements and change their position according to where the ball has gone, so they can intercept.

These are just a few examples of drills; many other interceptions or defensive drills that you can try out with your coach and teammates or practice on your own. Remember to practice your passing, dribbling, and positioning while working on your awareness in different areas of the field. By practicing these drills regularly, you can improve your awareness and become a better midfielder.

Train regularly and push yourself to improve your fitness level, work rate, and technical abilities. 2. Be a team player: Midfielders are the link between the defense and the attack. Work on your shooting skills: If you have an opportunity on goal, take your chances! Working on your shooting skills is essential to becoming a complete midfield player. 7. By following these tips and practicing regularly, you can become an excellent midfielder and contribute to the success of your team.

c83-m1.summary: ChannelCon 2016 is a key event for the IT channel
c83-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you provide more information about the upcoming ChannelCon 2016 event, including the keynote speaker and the types of sessions offered?
Generate according to: One of the best things about the IT channel is the industry community. With a few exceptions, the IT channel is made up essentially of small-business owners seeking to support the technology needs of other small businesses. That environment invites peer collaboration to ensure one is running a healthy business while providing customers with the best solutions and support.
It can take years of channel experience and a fair amount of relationship building to create the right environment. Partners come and go, as do staff members. All solution providers have to find their proper niches and develop the relationships, internal and external, to support the needs of their specific clients.
That isn't easy to do. While most IT business owners are truly technological gurus, able to navigate and design the most complex networks and security apps, they often struggle with balance sheets, partner negotiations and HR matters. Recruiting employees and developing long-term organizational plans is not in their comfort zone.
The good news is that most providers can overcome all those challenges. Whether they pick up best practices from peers or other industry professionals, or attend business-oriented training classes that help them master new skills, our industry offers a host of resources that can help.
CompTIA has been developing channel resources (for vendors and distributors, too) for decades. What started with our certifications programs--which continue to enable and drive the tech side of the industry--has extended into channel business training, peer communities, practice development programs and many other educational resources for IT professionals.
CompTIA's ChannelCon 2016, running from Aug. 1 to 3 in Hollywood, Fla., includes an agenda packed with training sessions and face-to-face peer community meetings.
One of the main attractions at the conference will be a keynote speech by Super Bowl champion and future NFL Hall of Famer Peyton Manning on game planning. Expect some insight on teamwork and skills development, as well as a few great stories from his memorable career.
Building a game-winning strategy for your IT business may not seem as glamorous as standing in the huddle during Super Bowl 50, but it's extremely important to those who depend on your support. Your clients and their customers, as well as your employees and their family members, all depend on your strategy's success.
Executive Certificate Courses: These classroom-style interactive sessions are structured around proven industry best practices and information gleaned from some of the top channel experts. If you're interested in acquiring valued business acumen that can be implemented right away, consider signing up for the intermediate-level Executive Certificate in Cloud. For our vendor members, there's the Executive Certificate in Channel Management track.
Specialty tracks: Struggling with talent recruitment? Check out the Behavioral Interviewing session at ChannelCon. Another session will show you how to sell security without the fear factor. Or you can sit in on a number of other channel-business enablement classes.
Community sessions: Who better to learn from that your peers? Our member communities and councils work year-round to drive positive change in the IT channel, and these interactive sessions get everyone involved. All channel professionals are welcome to attend, collaborate and discuss common industry issues. Just check out the schedules listed on the individual Community Web pages.
Tack4Techs: For the technical support team, these courses cover IT-specific education in sales and customer service, plus many of the soft skills they need to succeed in today’s workplace. The professional trainers at ChannelCon will help your staff develop new skills and, if they hold certain CompTIA certifications, they can earn continuing education unit, or CEU, credit as well.
Kelly Ricker is ‎senior vice president of events and education at CompTIA.

The conference, held from August 1-3 in Hollywood, Florida, invites attendees to participate in a variety of training sessions and peer community meetings. One of the highlights of the conference is the keynote speech presented by Super Bowl champion, Peyton Manning, who will speak on game planning and teamwork. The conference offers Executive Certificate Courses, specialty tracks, Community sessions and Tack4Techs courses that focus on providing IT-specific education in sales and customer service. The event is an excellent opportunity for attendees to learn new skills, collaborate with peers, and expand their knowledge on business-oriented training classes that will help their businesses grow.

c83-m8.summary: ChannelCon 2016 offers a variety of training sessions and peer communities.
c83-m8.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you provide more information about the upcoming ChannelCon 2016 event, including the keynote speaker and the types of sessions offered?
Generate according to: One of the best things about the IT channel is the industry community. With a few exceptions, the IT channel is made up essentially of small-business owners seeking to support the technology needs of other small businesses. That environment invites peer collaboration to ensure one is running a healthy business while providing customers with the best solutions and support.
It can take years of channel experience and a fair amount of relationship building to create the right environment. Partners come and go, as do staff members. All solution providers have to find their proper niches and develop the relationships, internal and external, to support the needs of their specific clients.
That isn't easy to do. While most IT business owners are truly technological gurus, able to navigate and design the most complex networks and security apps, they often struggle with balance sheets, partner negotiations and HR matters. Recruiting employees and developing long-term organizational plans is not in their comfort zone.
The good news is that most providers can overcome all those challenges. Whether they pick up best practices from peers or other industry professionals, or attend business-oriented training classes that help them master new skills, our industry offers a host of resources that can help.
CompTIA has been developing channel resources (for vendors and distributors, too) for decades. What started with our certifications programs--which continue to enable and drive the tech side of the industry--has extended into channel business training, peer communities, practice development programs and many other educational resources for IT professionals.
CompTIA's ChannelCon 2016, running from Aug. 1 to 3 in Hollywood, Fla., includes an agenda packed with training sessions and face-to-face peer community meetings.
One of the main attractions at the conference will be a keynote speech by Super Bowl champion and future NFL Hall of Famer Peyton Manning on game planning. Expect some insight on teamwork and skills development, as well as a few great stories from his memorable career.
Building a game-winning strategy for your IT business may not seem as glamorous as standing in the huddle during Super Bowl 50, but it's extremely important to those who depend on your support. Your clients and their customers, as well as your employees and their family members, all depend on your strategy's success.
Executive Certificate Courses: These classroom-style interactive sessions are structured around proven industry best practices and information gleaned from some of the top channel experts. If you're interested in acquiring valued business acumen that can be implemented right away, consider signing up for the intermediate-level Executive Certificate in Cloud. For our vendor members, there's the Executive Certificate in Channel Management track.
Specialty tracks: Struggling with talent recruitment? Check out the Behavioral Interviewing session at ChannelCon. Another session will show you how to sell security without the fear factor. Or you can sit in on a number of other channel-business enablement classes.
Community sessions: Who better to learn from that your peers? Our member communities and councils work year-round to drive positive change in the IT channel, and these interactive sessions get everyone involved. All channel professionals are welcome to attend, collaborate and discuss common industry issues. Just check out the schedules listed on the individual Community Web pages.
Tack4Techs: For the technical support team, these courses cover IT-specific education in sales and customer service, plus many of the soft skills they need to succeed in today’s workplace. The professional trainers at ChannelCon will help your staff develop new skills and, if they hold certain CompTIA certifications, they can earn continuing education unit, or CEU, credit as well.

c89-m1.summary: The user is interested in learning about history.
c89-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I need some help with a topic I'm interested in.
Assistant: What topic are you interested in? I'd be happy to help.
User: I'm thinking of learning more about history. Do you think it's an interesting subject?
Assistant: History can be fascinating. There's so much to learn from the past, and it can also help us understand the present. What specific area of history are you interested in?
User: Hmm, that's a good question. I'm not sure yet. I've always liked learning about old buildings and landmarks in my area.
Assistant: Local history can be particularly interesting because it's more relatable and tangible. You can visit the places you're learning about and see the historical sites firsthand.
User: Exactly! I think that's what draws me to it. But I've met someone recently who takes it to a whole new level.
Assistant: Oh? What do you mean?
User: Well, this person is just so passionate about local history. They seem to know everything about it.
Assistant: That sounds like a great resource for you! Having someone to talk to who is knowledgeable about the subject can be really helpful.
User: Yeah, but it's more than that. This person is obsessed with local history. They can tell you the smallest details about every building, every street, and every event that's ever happened in our town.
Assistant: Wow, that does sound like a high level of enthusiasm. While it's great that they're so interested, it can also be a bit overwhelming. How do you find interacting with this person?
User: Honestly, it's a bit exhausting. They can go on for hours about the history of a single building, and they get really excited about it.
Assistant: I can imagine. It's great that they're so passionate, but it's also important to have boundaries and be able to have a conversation that's not just about one topic. Have you tried talking to them about anything else?
User: Yeah, I've tried, but they always manage to steer the conversation back to local history. I'm starting to think that's all they care about.
Assistant: That can be challenging. It might be helpful to set some boundaries or find ways to politely change the subject. But at the same time, it's also interesting to learn from someone who is so knowledgeable about a particular topic. Maybe you can find ways to appreciate their enthusiasm while also maintaining your own interests and boundaries.
User: Hi, I'm feeling a bit down lately and I'm not sure what's wrong with me. I just can't seem to get excited about anything.
Assistant: I'm sorry to hear that. It can be really tough to feel unmotivated and disconnected from things. Can you tell me more about what's been going on? What are some things that you used to enjoy doing, but don't feel like doing anymore?
User: Well, I used to love going for walks and trying out new restaurants, but lately, I just don't feel like leaving the house. And even when I do, I don't really enjoy myself.
Assistant: That sounds really challenging. Have you noticed any patterns or changes in your mood or energy levels over the past few months? For example, do you feel more tired or sluggish at certain times of the day or year?
User: Now that you mention it, I do feel more tired and sluggish during the winter months. I just thought it was because of the cold weather, but maybe there's more to it.
Assistant: That's a good observation. The winter months can be tough for a lot of people, especially with the shorter days and colder temperatures. Some people experience something called Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), which is a type of depression that's related to the changing seasons. Do you think that might be something that's affecting you?
User: Actually, I think that might be exactly what's going on. I've been struggling with this for years, but I never knew what it was. I just thought I was being lazy or something.
Assistant: Not at all! SAD is a real condition that affects a lot of people. It's not about being lazy or anything like that. It's just that your body is responding to the changing seasons in a way that's affecting your mood and energy levels. There are things we can do to help manage it, though. Have you tried using a light therapy lamp or doing any activities that help you feel more energized and motivated during the winter months?
User: No, I haven't tried anything like that. But I'm willing to try anything at this point. What are some things that might help?
Assistant: Well, light therapy lamps can be really helpful because they mimic the sunlight that we don't get as much of during the winter months. Exercise can also be really helpful, especially if you can find activities that you enjoy doing indoors. And some people find it helpful to plan fun activities or trips during the winter months to give them something to look forward to. What do you think might work for you?
User: I think the light therapy lamp might be a good idea. And maybe I can try to find some indoor activities that I enjoy, like yoga or something. But what about the days when I just don't feel like doing anything at all?
Assistant: Those days can be really tough. One thing that might help is to break things down into smaller, more manageable tasks. Instead of feeling like you need to do a whole workout or clean the whole house, maybe just start with one small thing, like taking a short walk or doing one load of laundry. Sometimes, just getting started can help you build momentum and feel more energized. And it's also okay to have days when you just don't feel like doing anything at all. Allow yourself to rest and take care of yourself, and don't beat yourself up over it.
User: That makes sense. I think I can try to do that. But what if I'm still feeling really down and struggling to motivate myself? What should I do then?
Assistant: If you're still feeling really down and struggling to motivate yourself, it might be helpful to talk to a therapist or counselor who can provide you with additional support and guidance. They can help you develop coping strategies and work through any underlying issues that might be contributing to your SAD. And if you're feeling really overwhelmed or struggling to take care of yourself, don't hesitate to reach out to a crisis hotline or emergency services for support.
User: Okay, I think I'll look into that. Thank you for talking with me and helping me understand what's going on. I feel a little better just knowing that there's a name for what I'm experiencing and that there are things I can do to help manage it.
Assistant: You're welcome! I'm glad I could help. Remember that you're not alone in this, and there are people and resources available to support you. Take care of yourself and don't hesitate to reach out if you need anything.

c101-m1.summary: The Women’s History Research Journal includes editable sections for adding your own questions.
c101-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you summarize the different sources for researching family genealogy mentioned in the text?
Generate according to: The question, "how can I find my family history" is fairly easily answered, but the answer itself is fairly complex-not because the sources for family genealogy are so limited but because they are so plentiful. Ways to research the family history are limited to three-archives, relatives and of course the ever-present internet, but within those ways are incredibly diverse pathways to genealogical research.
The highest and best accolades go to Rootsweb, an online database (under the aegis of World Connect Project) which has a stunning amount of data behind it. This one-stop shopper of a website allows researchers to upload family trees which they can subsequently modify (to emphasize a certain branch) then link and share out in display for other family members or fellow researchers.
Rootsweb is somewhat unique in that not only is it the largest database out there, but also it allows individuals to add to or remove information to allow for family births, deaths, events and similar updates. This greatly increases the probability that current and reliable information is on the site, and the database (which is free), with 3 billion names and over three hundred thousand detailed family trees, probably cannot be bested as an immediate research source for any family genealogy, whether one is researching a single member of a single branch or creating an extensive family history.
A major social force that practices family genealogical study, not only for information but as the basis of faith, is Mormonism, so it's not surprising that the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints should offer the website FamilySearch, which is free to all genealogists regardless of religious persuasion. The databases are centered on sites of Mormonism in the US, but they provide wonderful image quality and an extensive set of indexes, as well as the records of numerous countries worldwide.
A third (and often overlooked) source of family history is governmental: the U.S. Federal Land Patent Records website, located on the website for the Bureau of Land Management, is another excellent, free and comprehensive database, with access to Federal land records, as well as images of contracts, titles and all kinds of delightful genealogical clues for family detectives, all the way back to 1820. It features not only an index to land purchases but also the actual documents themselves, and is an invaluable site for people whose ancestors were able to buy land in any contractual arrangement.
Finally, there's the invaluable (if slightly depressing) death records that one can search for family history and loved ones that time and memory may have obscured. Interment.net is very likely to have extensive details about at least one of the ancestors in anyone's family tree. There are over 3 million records contained in this little site, from over five thousand cemeteries listed worldwide. And Internment.net actually has all the available cemetery and funerary transcriptions, as well as links to other transcriptions from other cemeteries. It's truly a global site that specializes in the records of the long departed and sometimes forgotten, and it's a great place to revive and revisit loved ones and old memories.
These are three websites that answer the question, "How can I find my family history?"
Assistant: Rootsweb, FamilySearch, and the US Federal Land Patent Records website are three websites that offer comprehensive and free databases for researching family genealogy. Rootsweb is the largest and most extensive, with the ability to upload and modify family trees, making it an excellent immediate research source. FamilySearch is a website centered on Mormonism but offers excellent image quality and indexes, as well as records from numerous countries worldwide. The US Federal Land Patent Records website provides valuable clues for family detectives, including the actual documents themselves, back to 1820. Lastly, Interment.net offers over 3 million records from worldwide cemeteries, making it an invaluable source for finding loved ones and old memories.
User: Can you give me a brief overview of the databases available on FamilySearch?
Assistant: FamilySearch is a free genealogy website that offers access to an extensive collection of databases and records from around the world. The databases available on FamilySearch include vital records, census records, military records, church records, and more. Some of the notable databases include the U.S. Census from 1790 to 1940, the International Genealogical Index, and the Pedigree Resource File. FamilySearch also offers access to collections specific to certain regions, such as European records or Latin American records. Users can search these databases and records for free and access images of original documents when available. FamilySearch is a valuable resource for anyone looking to research their family history.

c103-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Given the text: Uh-oh… How can you end up with three different birth-dates from Grandpa Burt? And five possible marriage dates for Aunt Ernestine? Genealogy research is rarely cut-and-dried, and sometimes it’s difficult to know which record is most likely correct. But Christine Rose helps you weigh and analyze your sources in Genealogical Proof Standard: Building a Solid Case (CR Publications, $8.95). This guide packs a lot of solid advice into 58 pages, showing you step by step in case studies how to evaluate evidence and resolve your genealogical discrepancies. It’s a must-read for all genealogists.
HOT OFF THE PRESS:New books to heat up your family history search.
1. One day, you’ll become an ancestor. What are you leaving for your descendants? In You Don’t Have to Be Famous (Writer’s Digest Books), Steve Zousmer takes the intimidation out of writing your life story, so you can leave a legacy for future generations. Zousmer’s message: Whether or not you’ve led an adventurous life, your life story is meaningful because it’s unique. Get going with this practical guide.
2. Combining history, biography and memoir, Bill Griffeth traces his family tree through the history of Protestantism. By Faith Alone: One Family’s Epic Journey Through 400 Years of American Protestantism (Harmony Books) follows Griffeth as he travels to England, the Netherlands and Massachusetts in search of his roots — and discovers how faith shaped his ancestors’ lives as well as his own.
3. Between 1761 and 1853, a steady stream of Irish came to Canada. Erin’s Sons: Irish Arrivals in Atlantic Canada, 1761-1853 by Terrence M. Punch (Genealogical Publishing Co.), offers listings of those Irish immigrants from passenger lists; censuses; newspapers; military, church and prison records; and tombstone inscriptions. The book also gives a brief history of Irish settlement in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador.
• Recommended by: Laura G. Prescott, vice president of the Association of Professional Genealogists <apgen.org> and a 10-year genealogy veteran.
• Book summary: As its tide indicates, this book is about the settling of North America, from before recorded time to the end of the 1700s.
• Likes and dislikes: I admire the writer’s storytelling style. Too many people are ignorant of history because it’s often presented in a dull manner. Morgan makes it exciting and relevant — presenting not only influential characters but also leading roles played by the common man (and woman).
• Behind the scenes: While at Dartmouth, I naively focused my history major on Europe, not realizing how much of our nation’s history my ancestors experienced or helped shape. After I immersed myself in genealogy, I discovered it’s vital to have a deep understanding of American history to create family histories and understand the records we use.
• Lasting impressions: Anyone working with US families — especially those with early American roots — needs a good awareness of events, social patterns and historical trends to locate records, decipher relationships, and appreciate an individual’s or family’s role. This book is a terrific primer for these purposes.
• Best bonus: This book has given me a better appreciation of the roles our ancestors played in shaping the continent’s cities, hinterlands and wilderness.

• Best bonus: This book has given me a better appreciation of the roles our ancestors played in shaping the continent’s cities, hinterlands and wilderness.

c105-m1.summary: The world doesn't stop turning as soon as your catch your cap.
c105-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Given the text: Well, believe it or not, the world doesn’t stop turning as soon as your catch your cap. Its a big and exciting world out there and to help prove our point, we’re starting a new miniseries of articles called Meet the Graduates.
The point of this isn’t to make a few recent grads famous or to inflate anybody’s ego, but to demonstrate the wealth of opportunities available to you, and some pitfalls to avoid.
He’s the one with the lion’s mane of hair.
After gradation I was depressed. I had achieved what I wanted to achieve at uni, but my life didn’t suddenly fall into place as I had envisioned it. While a part of me had known that the idea of a smooth transition to working life without any concrete plans was a fantasy, dealing with the reality of the situation was difficult to cope with. If anything, the fact that I had done well on my course made this experience harder, as I felt that I felt more pressured to find a ‘good’ job.
Speaking from personal experience, I know how easy it is for your mental health to slip after graduation, which is why it’s important to plan ahead of time.
Did you get a job relating to your course?
The market for jobs related specifically to history is narrow and mostly related to academia, but the amount of jobs which utilise history-related skills is extensive. During my time at Uni I became interested by prospect of a career in the Foreign Office. Transition to a Civil Service job is a fairly common practice amongst History graduates, as the ‘transferable skills’ jargon careers officers use is not as BS as it sounds. However, I decided to postpone my application to the Foreign Office until after I get an MA and improve my language skills.
How long did it take you to find a job after graduation?
After prioritising enjoying my summer aftergraduation, I found a job at a law firm later in the year.
I was still dealing with the sense of aimlessness following my graduation. The job itself was tedious and I only did it because it sounded respectable, rather than being something I was genuinely interested in pursuing.
Don’t take the first job you’re offered, just because it’s the first job you’re offered.
Tyfy can help you build up a portfolio of reviews on your emlpyability skills in your spare time, to try to ease you into the real world.
So, how did you get out of the rut?
I decided to re-evaluate how I was planning my future. Rather than focusing on specific career goals, I decided to prioritise working on myself and improving some of my weaker qualities. I had always been shy and struggled to be assertive in a group, so I decided to work in a school as I felt if I could get a class of 30 angsty teens to follow my instructions, then I’d gain the confidence to speak up amongst more reasonable adults.
So here’s the second piece of advice – It’s okay to be out of your comfort zone once you graduate, and being there helps you find what you do want to do.
After working as an SEN TA for the majority of a school year, I realised that I wanted to go back to academia and do a Masters, so now I’m back at UCL, , I had a great relationship with the teaching staff during my undergrad and so I wanted to come back. The course also allowed me to study the parts of history that I’m most passionate about – 20th Century Africa and South America – and has access to a bunch of fantastic resources.
I would have encouraged myself to actually go to the societies that I signed up for in first year, to meet new people and do things I may not get a chance to after uni, especially for such low costs.
If you feel anxious about what you’re going to do after Uni, talk to someone about it, particularly your Uni’s career service. If you’ve already graduated and feel lost, don’t put so much pressure on yourself. It’s great to see your friends do well after they graduate, but remember that you’re still young and that just because you don’t have a concrete career plan now, that doesn’t mean that you won’t in the future. Also, if you feel overwhelmingly depressed or anxious at any point, be brave enough to be as open as you can, it’s hard but talking about your feelings definitely helps.
Can you provide some tips for recent graduates who are struggling with post-graduation depression and aimlessness?
Assistant: 1. Don't put too much pressure on yourself to have a concrete career plan right after graduation.
2. Talk to someone about your feelings, especially the Uni's career service.
3. Take some time to work on yourself and improve weaker qualities.
4. Don't take the first job you're offered just because it sounds respectable.
5. Step out of your comfort zone and try new things.
6. Try to build up a portfolio of reviews on your employability skills in your spare time.
7. Remember that your mental health is important and seek help if you need it.

The point of this isn’t to make a few recent grads famous or to inflate anybody’s ego, but to demonstrate the wealth of opportunities available to you, and some pitfalls to avoid.
He’s the one with the lion’s mane of hair.
After gradation I was depressed. I had achieved what I wanted to achieve at uni, but my life didn’t suddenly fall into place as I had envisioned it. While a part of me had known that the idea of a smooth transition to working life without any concrete plans was a fantasy, dealing with the reality of the situation was difficult to cope with. If anything, the fact that I had done well on my course made this experience harder, as I felt that I felt more pressured to find a ‘good’ job.
Speaking from personal experience, I know how easy it is for your mental health to slip after graduation, which is why it’s important to plan ahead of time.
Did you get a job relating to your course?
The market for jobs related specifically to history is narrow and mostly related to academia, but the amount of jobs which utilise history-related skills is extensive. Transition to a Civil Service job is a fairly common practice amongst History graduates, as the ‘transferable skills’ jargon careers officers use is not as BS as it sounds. However, I decided to postpone my application to the Foreign Office until after I get an MA and improve my language skills.
How long did it take you to find a job after graduation?
After prioritising enjoying my summer aftergraduation, I found a job at a law firm later in the year.
I was still dealing with the sense of aimlessness following my graduation. The job itself was tedious and I only did it because it sounded respectable, rather than being something I was genuinely interested in pursuing.
Don’t take the first job you’re offered, just because it’s the first job you’re offered.

I had always been shy and struggled to be assertive in a group, so I decided to work in a school as I felt if I could get a class of 30 angsty teens to follow my instructions, then I’d gain the confidence to speak up amongst more reasonable adults.

I would have encouraged myself to actually go to the societies that I signed up for in first year, to meet new people and do things I may not get a chance to after uni, especially for such low costs.
